definition: In a way that is so plainly true that no one could reasonably argue against it.
example: The new bridge is undeniably faster than the old ferry route across the bay.
nuance: Undeniably marks a claim as beyond dispute, while arguably admits that reasonable people might still disagree.
prompt: A coach reviews the season's results with the team at the final meeting.
options: After twelve wins and no losses, this was undeniably the team's best season.
The referee couldn't tell who touched the ball last, so it was undeniably a foul.
When asked for an extra practice, the coach undeniably said no and walked away.
Since anything can happen, next year's team will undeniably win every game.
reasons: A perfect record is plain evidence that nobody could reasonably dispute.
A call the referee could not see clearly is open to dispute, not beyond it.
The word does not mean refusing; it signals certainty about a fact, not a rejection.
Admitting that anything can happen makes the prediction uncertain, not indisputable.

practice.prompt: A science class measures how fast ice cubes melt in sunlight and in shade.
options: The cubes in the sun undeniably melted first; every group's timer agreed.
The data was messy and confusing, so the results were undeniably clear.
One student undeniably rejected his partner's idea and refused to help.
Before taking any measurements, the teacher guessed the shaded cube would undeniably last longer.
reasons: Matching results from every group leave no room for argument.
Messy, confusing data cannot support a conclusion that is beyond question.
This treats the word as a kind of refusal; it describes certainty, not saying no.
A guess made before collecting evidence is speculation, not something proven.
